tool.name: Spring Boot
tool.tagline: Opinionated Java framework for production-ready web services and apps
tool.description: Spring Boot builds on the Spring Framework to create stand-alone, production-ready Java applications with minimal configuration: starters pull in consistent dependencies, auto-configuration wires sensible defaults, and an embedded server runs the app as a plain jar. It is the most widely used way to build REST APIs, microservices and data-backed backends on the JVM. Learning it means learning dependency injection, Spring MVC, Spring Data, testing and operations the way most Java teams practise them.

concepts.name: Creating a Spring Boot app
concepts.summary: Generate a project with Spring Initializr, understand starters and @SpringBootApplication, and run it.
concepts.why: Every Spring Boot project starts from this structure, and knowing what each piece does demystifies the framework.
concepts.body:
The quickest start is **Spring Initializr** (start.spring.io, or built into IntelliJ and VS Code): pick Maven or Gradle, Java 17+ (Boot 3 requires 17; 21 is a good choice), and add dependencies such as *Spring Web*. You get a project with a build file, a main class, `application.properties` and a test.

Dependencies come as **starters**: `spring-boot-starter-web` brings Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON and an embedded Tomcat; `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` brings Hibernate and Spring Data. The Spring Boot parent POM (or Gradle plugin) manages compatible versions, so you rarely write version numbers yourself.

The main class is annotated `@SpringBootApplication`, which combines three things:

- `@Configuration`: the class can define beans.
- `@EnableAutoConfiguration`: Boot configures components based on what's on the classpath (Tomcat and Spring MVC appear because the web starter is there).
- `@ComponentScan`: classes annotated `@Component`, `@Service`, `@RestController` and so on, in this package **and its sub-packages**, are discovered.

`SpringApplication.run(App.class, args)` creates the application context, starts the embedded server (port 8080 by default) and keeps running. Put the main class in a root package such as `com.example.shop` so scanning finds everything below it.
takeaways: Starters bundle consistent dependencies; Boot manages their versions
`@SpringBootApplication` = configuration + auto-configuration + component scan
Component scanning covers the main class's package and sub-packages
The embedded server makes the app a self-contained process
pitfalls: Putting the main class in a sub-package, so controllers in sibling packages are never scanned.

quiz.q: Why is a @RestController in com.example.web not found when the main class is in com.example.app?
options: Controllers must be in the same file
@RestController needs to be registered in application.properties
Component scanning starts at the main class's package and only covers its sub-packages
quiz.explain: @SpringBootApplication scans its own package downwards; com.example.web is a sibling, not a sub-package.

concepts.name: Beans and dependency injection
concepts.summary: Let the Spring container create your objects (beans) and inject their dependencies through constructors.
concepts.why: Dependency injection is the core of Spring; every other feature is built on beans.
concepts.body:
Spring's **application context** (the IoC container) creates and manages objects called **beans**. Instead of calling `new` for your services, you declare them and let the container wire them together.

Two ways to declare beans:

- Annotate a class with a **stereotype**: `@Component`, or the more descriptive `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`/`@RestController`. Component scanning registers it.
- Write a `@Bean` method in a `@Configuration` class, for objects from libraries you can't annotate or that need custom construction.

Dependencies are injected through the **constructor**: declare a `final` field and a constructor parameter, and Spring passes the matching bean. With a single constructor no `@Autowired` is needed. Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, allows immutability and makes classes easy to test with plain `new`. Field injection (`@Autowired` on a field) still works but hides dependencies and is discouraged.

Depend on **interfaces** where it helps: inject `PaymentGateway`, not `StripeGateway`. If several beans implement the interface, pick one with `@Primary` or `@Qualifier("name")`, or inject `List<PaymentGateway>` to get them all.

Beans are **singletons** by default: one shared instance per context, so they must be stateless or thread-safe.
takeaways: The container creates beans and injects their dependencies
Use stereotypes for your classes and `@Bean` methods for library objects
Prefer constructor injection with final fields
Beans are singletons by default, so keep them stateless
pitfalls: Storing per-request data in a field of a singleton @Service, which is shared across all requests.

quiz.q: A @Service has one constructor taking a Notifier. What do you need for Spring to inject it?
options: Nothing: a single constructor is used automatically
quiz.explain: Since Spring 4.3 a class with a single constructor gets it autowired without any annotation.

concepts.name: application.properties and @Value
concepts.summary: Configure your app and Boot's components with application.properties or YAML, and read values with @Value.
concepts.why: Externalised configuration lets the same jar run in dev, test and production.
takeaways: `application.properties`/`.yml` configure Boot and your own code
Environment variables and command-line args override packaged values
`@Value("${key:default}")` injects one value
Keep secrets out of the repository
pitfalls: Hard-coding environment-specific URLs in the jar instead of overriding them per environment.

quiz.q: application.properties sets server.port=8080 and the environment has SERVER_PORT=9000. Which port is used?
quiz.explain: Environment variables have higher precedence than packaged properties, and relaxed binding maps SERVER_PORT to server.port.

concepts.name: Building and running the jar
concepts.summary: Run during development with the Maven or Gradle plugin, package an executable jar and use DevTools.
concepts.why: You need a fast dev loop and a deployable artifact.
concepts.body:
The Spring Boot build plugin does two jobs. During development, `./mvnw spring-boot:run` (or `./gradlew bootRun`) starts the app from source. For deployment, `./mvnw package` (or `./gradlew bootJar`) produces an **executable fat jar** in `target/` that contains your classes, all dependency jars and a small launcher, runnable anywhere with a JVM: `java -jar target/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar`.

Use the wrapper scripts (`mvnw`, `gradlew`) that Initializr generates, so everyone builds with the same tool version.

**DevTools** (`spring-boot-devtools`, a development-only dependency) restarts the application automatically when classes change on the classpath, which is much faster than a cold start, and disables template caching. It is excluded from packaged jars automatically.

For containers, `./mvnw spring-boot:build-image` builds an OCI image with Cloud Native Buildpacks, no Dockerfile required. If you write your own Dockerfile, extract the jar into layers (`java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers`) so dependency layers are cached between builds.

At startup the log shows the active profiles, the port and the startup time, and `--debug` prints the auto-configuration report, useful when something isn't configured the way you expect.
concepts.code:
# development
./mvnw spring-boot:run                      # or: ./gradlew bootRun

# package an executable jar and run it
./mvnw clean package
java -jar target/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --server.port=9090

# container image via buildpacks (needs Docker)
./mvnw spring-boot:build-image -Dspring-boot.build-image.imageName=shop:latest
docker run -p 8080:8080 shop:latest

# see why things were (not) auto-configured
java -jar target/shop-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar --debug | grep -A3 "Positive matches"
takeaways: `spring-boot:run`/`bootRun` for development, `package`/`bootJar` for a fat jar
The fat jar runs anywhere with `java -jar`
DevTools restarts on change and is dropped from production jars
`build-image` creates a container image without a Dockerfile
pitfalls: Deploying the plain (non-repackaged) jar, which lacks dependencies and fails with ClassNotFoundException.

quiz.q: What makes the Spring Boot jar executable with java -jar?
options: The plugin repackages it with all dependencies and a launcher main class
quiz.explain: The Boot plugin repackages the jar with nested dependency jars and a launcher that sets up the classpath.

concepts.name: REST controllers and request mapping
concepts.summary: Map HTTP requests to methods with @RestController, @GetMapping, @PathVariable and @RequestParam.
concepts.why: REST APIs are the most common thing built with Spring Boot.
concepts.body:
A class annotated `@RestController` handles HTTP requests; each method's return value is serialised to the response body, as JSON by default via Jackson. `@RequestMapping("/api/books")` on the class sets a common path prefix.

Methods are mapped with `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@PatchMapping` and `@DeleteMapping`. Parameters bind parts of the request:

- `@PathVariable Long id` takes `{id}` from the path `/api/books/{id}` and converts it to the declared type; a failed conversion gives a 400.
- `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page` reads `?page=2`. Parameters are required unless they have a default or `required = false` (or are `Optional`).
- `@RequestHeader` reads headers.

Return a domain object, a `List`, or a Java **record**: Jackson turns record components into JSON fields. To control status and headers, return `ResponseEntity<T>`: `ResponseEntity.ok(book)` or `ResponseEntity.notFound().build()`.

Controllers should be thin: translate HTTP to method calls on a `@Service` and back. Business logic in controllers is hard to test and reuse.

Spring MVC runs each request on a thread from Tomcat's pool (or a virtual thread if enabled), so controllers must be stateless, like all singleton beans.
takeaways: `@RestController` methods return objects serialised to JSON
`@PathVariable` binds path segments, `@RequestParam` query parameters
Return `ResponseEntity` to control status codes and headers
Keep controllers thin; delegate to services
pitfalls: Returning null for a missing resource, which gives 200 with an empty body instead of 404.

quiz.q: A method has @RequestParam int page with no default and the request has no page parameter. What happens?
options: The request fails with 400 Bad Request
quiz.explain: Request parameters are required by default; a missing one is a client error unless a default or required = false is set.

concepts.name: Request bodies and status codes
concepts.summary: Accept JSON with @RequestBody, return 201 Created with a Location header, and handle PUT and DELETE.
concepts.why: Creating and updating resources is half of every REST API.
concepts.body:
For `POST`, `PUT` and `PATCH`, the client sends JSON in the body. Annotate a parameter with `@RequestBody` and Jackson deserialises it into your type. Records work well as request DTOs: immutable, concise, and the JSON field names match the component names. Unknown JSON properties are ignored by default in Spring Boot; malformed JSON gives 400.

Use separate DTOs for input and output rather than exposing your JPA entities directly. That keeps clients from setting fields like `id` or `createdAt`, and lets the API evolve independently of the database.

Status codes matter:

- `201 Created` with a `Location` header after creating something: `ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto)`. `ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest().path("/{id}")` builds the URI.
- `204 No Content` after a successful delete or an update that returns nothing: `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()`, or annotate the method with `@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)`.
- `404` when the target doesn't exist, `409` for conflicts.

`PUT` replaces a resource and should be idempotent; `PATCH` changes part of it. Keep them semantically correct and clients (and caches and retries) behave predictably.

Test quickly with `curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{...}'` or an HTTP client in your IDE.
takeaways: `@RequestBody` deserialises JSON into a DTO (records work well)
Use separate request/response DTOs instead of entities
Return 201 + Location on create, 204 on delete, 404 when missing
pitfalls: Binding request bodies straight to JPA entities, letting clients overwrite ids or internal fields.

quiz.q: Which response best fits a successful POST that created a resource?
options: 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource
quiz.explain: 201 with Location tells the client the resource was created and where to find it.

concepts.name: Spring Data JPA repositories
concepts.summary: Map entities with JPA annotations and get CRUD and derived queries from repository interfaces.
concepts.why: Most Spring Boot services persist data in a relational database through Spring Data JPA.
concepts.body:
Add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` and a JDBC driver (PostgreSQL, MySQL, or H2 for experiments). Boot configures a connection pool (HikariCP), Hibernate as the JPA provider and transaction management from the `spring.datasource.*` properties.

An **entity** is a class annotated `@Entity` with an `@Id` (often `@GeneratedValue`). Fields map to columns; `@Column`, `@Table` and relationship annotations (`@ManyToOne`, `@OneToMany`) customise the mapping. Entities need a no-argument constructor (it can be `protected`), and they are mutable classes, not records.

A **repository** is just an interface: `interface BookRepository extends JpaRepository<Book, Long> {}`. Spring Data generates the implementation at startup with `save`, `findById` (returns `Optional`), `findAll`, `deleteById`, `count`, paging and sorting.

**Derived queries** come from method names: `findByAuthor(String a)`, `findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase(String s)`, `countByPublishedAfter(LocalDate d)`, `findTop5ByOrderByPublishedDesc()`. A typo in the name fails at startup, not at runtime. For anything complex, write JPQL with `@Query("select b from Book b where ...")`.

Schema management: `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` defaults to `create-drop` for embedded databases only. For real databases manage the schema with **Flyway** or **Liquibase** migrations, and keep `ddl-auto=validate` or `none`.
takeaways: `@Entity` + `@Id` maps a class to a table
Extend `JpaRepository<T, ID>` and get CRUD, paging and sorting for free
Derived query methods are parsed from names and checked at startup
Use Flyway or Liquibase for schema changes, not ddl-auto
pitfalls: Using spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update in production, which can't handle renames and drifts silently.

quiz.q: What does Spring Data do with a method List<Book> findByAuthor(String author) in a repository interface?
options: Generates a query filtering on the author property
Calls a stored procedure named findByAuthor
quiz.explain: Derived queries are built from the method name, here where author = ?.

concepts.name: Testing with @SpringBootTest and @WebMvcTest
concepts.summary: Write unit tests without Spring, slice tests for controllers with MockMvc, and full integration tests.
concepts.why: Fast, focused tests are what make Spring applications safe to change.
concepts.body:
`spring-boot-starter-test` brings JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito and Spring's test support. Use three kinds of test:

- **Plain unit tests** for services: thanks to constructor injection, `new SignupService(fakeNotifier, clock)` needs no Spring at all. These are the fastest and should be the majority.
- **Slice tests** load only one layer. `@WebMvcTest(BookController.class)` starts just the MVC infrastructure plus that controller and gives you a `MockMvc` to perform requests without a server. Its dependencies are replaced with mocks using `@MockitoBean` (Spring Framework 6.2+, replacing the deprecated `@MockBean`). `@DataJpaTest` similarly loads only JPA components with an embedded database, rolling back after each test.
- **Full integration tests** with `@SpringBootTest` start the whole application context. Add `webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT` to run a real server and call it with `TestRestTemplate` or `WebTestClient`.

MockMvc asserts on status, headers and JSON with `jsonPath("$.title").value("Dune")`. Spring caches application contexts between tests with the same configuration, so keep test configurations consistent to avoid slow context restarts.

Name tests after behaviour, test HTTP contracts at the controller layer (status codes, validation, JSON shape) and business rules at the service layer.
takeaways: Unit-test services with plain `new`; no Spring needed
`@WebMvcTest` + MockMvc tests controllers without a server
`@MockitoBean` swaps a bean for a Mockito mock
`@SpringBootTest` loads everything; use it sparingly
pitfalls: Using @SpringBootTest for every test, making the suite slow when slices or plain unit tests would do.

quiz.q: What does @WebMvcTest(BookController.class) load?
options: The entire application including the database
Nothing; it's a plain JUnit test
Only the MVC layer and BookController; other beans must be mocked
quiz.explain: It's a slice test: MVC infrastructure and the named controller, with collaborators supplied as mocks.

concepts.name: Validating input
concepts.summary: Validate request bodies and parameters with Jakarta Bean Validation annotations and @Valid.
concepts.why: Rejecting bad input at the edge keeps invalid data out of your services and database.
concepts.body:
Add `spring-boot-starter-validation` (Hibernate Validator). Then put **constraints** on DTO fields or record components: `@NotBlank`, `@NotNull`, `@Size(max = 100)`, `@Email`, `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Positive`, `@Past`, `@Pattern(regexp = ...)`. In Boot 3 they live in the `jakarta.validation.constraints` package (not `javax`).

Trigger validation by annotating the controller parameter with `@Valid` (or `@Validated`): `create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateUser req)`. If a constraint fails, the method isn't called and Spring throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which becomes a **400 Bad Request**. Customise the response body with an exception handler (next lesson).

Nested objects are validated only if the field itself is annotated `@Valid`. For `@PathVariable` and `@RequestParam` constraints (`@Min(1) @PathVariable long id`), Spring MVC 6.1+ applies method validation automatically when constraints are present.

Write custom constraints when the built-ins aren't enough: an annotation plus a `ConstraintValidator` class. Cross-field rules (end after start) can be a constraint on the class.

Validation in the web layer complements, but doesn't replace, database constraints and business-rule checks in services. You can also validate service methods with `@Validated` on the class, and `@ConfigurationProperties` classes the same way.
takeaways: Constraints like `@NotBlank`, `@Email`, `@Size` live in `jakarta.validation`
`@Valid` on the parameter triggers validation; failures give 400
Cascade into nested objects with `@Valid` on the field
Validation at the edge complements database constraints
pitfalls: Forgetting @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter, so all the constraint annotations are silently ignored.

quiz.q: A record has @NotBlank String name but the controller parameter is just @RequestBody CreateUser req. What happens with an empty name?
options: The request is accepted; nothing triggers validation
The name is set to null
quiz.explain: Constraints are only checked when validation is triggered, e.g. by @Valid on the parameter.

concepts.name: Error handling and ProblemDetail
concepts.summary: Map exceptions to HTTP responses with @RestControllerAdvice, @ExceptionHandler and RFC 9457 ProblemDetail.
concepts.why: Consistent error responses make APIs predictable for clients and keep controllers clean.
concepts.body:
When a controller throws, Spring looks for an **exception handler**. Methods annotated `@ExceptionHandler(SomeException.class)` in a `@RestControllerAdvice` class apply to all controllers, so error handling lives in one place and controllers only deal with the happy path.

Spring supports the **Problem Details** standard (RFC 9457, formerly RFC 7807) through the `ProblemDetail` class, producing `application/problem+json` bodies with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `instance`, plus custom properties. Set `spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true` to have Spring's own exceptions (400s for bad input, 405, 415 and so on) rendered this way too.

A typical setup:

- Define domain exceptions like `BookNotFoundException`.
- Map each to a status in the advice: `ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage())`.
- Extend `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` to customise Spring's built-in exceptions, for example to list validation errors from `MethodArgumentNotValidException`.
- Add a catch-all `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` that logs the error and returns a generic 500 without leaking stack traces.

Alternatively throw `ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "...")` directly for simple cases, or annotate an exception class with `@ResponseStatus`. Unhandled errors fall through to Boot's `/error` endpoint, which returns a basic JSON body.
takeaways: `@RestControllerAdvice` + `@ExceptionHandler` centralise error mapping
Return `ProblemDetail` for standard application/problem+json bodies
Map domain exceptions to statuses; never leak stack traces
`ResponseStatusException` covers simple one-off cases
pitfalls: Catching exceptions in every controller method and building error responses by hand, inconsistently.

quiz.q: Where should a handler live so it applies to exceptions from all controllers?
quiz.explain: @ControllerAdvice/@RestControllerAdvice handlers apply globally across controllers.

concepts.name: Typed configuration and profiles
concepts.summary: Bind groups of settings to validated @ConfigurationProperties records and switch environments with profiles.
concepts.why: Typed, validated configuration catches mistakes at startup instead of in production traffic.
concepts.body:
For a group of related settings, define a class or record annotated `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail")`. Boot binds `app.mail.host`, `app.mail.port`, `app.mail.from` and nested objects, lists, maps and `Duration`s (`timeout=5s`) to it with type conversion, and you inject it like any bean. Register it with `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` on the main class or `@EnableConfigurationProperties(MailProperties.class)`.

Benefits over scattered `@Value`s: one place for related settings, IDE auto-completion (with the `spring-boot-configuration-processor` dependency), and **validation** at startup with `@Validated` plus constraints: a missing host fails fast with a clear message.

**Profiles** select environment-specific configuration. `application-dev.properties` and `application-prod.properties` are loaded in addition to `application.properties` when the `dev` or `prod` profile is active, and override it. Activate with `spring.profiles.active=prod` (often via the environment variable `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`). A single YAML file can hold several profile sections separated by `---` with `spring.config.activate.on-profile`.

Beans can be profile-specific with `@Profile("dev")`, for example a fake payment gateway in development. Keep profiles few and about environments; feature switches belong in normal properties.
takeaways: `@ConfigurationProperties` binds a prefix to a typed record or class
`@Validated` + constraints fail fast at startup
`application-{profile}.properties` overrides the defaults for that profile
Activate profiles with `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`
pitfalls: Creating a profile per feature flag, leading to combinatorial configurations; use plain properties for flags.

quiz.q: The dev profile is active. application.properties sets app.mail.host=a and application-dev.properties sets it to b. What is bound?
quiz.explain: Profile-specific files are loaded after the default file and override its values.

concepts.name: Transactions with @Transactional
concepts.summary: Group database work into atomic units with @Transactional and understand rollback rules and propagation.
concepts.why: Without correct transaction boundaries, partial updates corrupt data under failures.
concepts.body:
Annotate a service method with `@Transactional` and Spring starts a transaction before the method and commits after it returns. If it throws, the transaction is **rolled back**. Everything the method does through repositories (and anything it calls in the same thread) shares that transaction and its database connection.

Rules that matter:

- By default only **unchecked** exceptions (`RuntimeException`, `Error`) trigger rollback. A checked exception commits unless you add `rollbackFor = Exception.class`.
- `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` for query methods lets Hibernate skip dirty checking and lets the driver route to replicas.
- **Propagation** decides what happens when a transactional method calls another: the default `REQUIRED` joins the existing transaction; `REQUIRES_NEW` suspends it and starts an independent one, useful for audit logs that must persist even if the outer work fails.
- Inside a transaction, loaded entities are **managed**: changing a field is written automatically at commit (dirty checking), no `save` call needed.

Transactions are implemented with **proxies**: the annotation only works when the method is called through the Spring bean from another bean. A call from one method to another `@Transactional` method in the **same class** bypasses the proxy, so the annotation on the inner method is ignored. Also, annotated methods should be public (Spring 6 also supports protected and package-private methods with class-based proxies).

Put transaction boundaries on service methods representing one use case, not on controllers or repositories.
takeaways: `@Transactional` commits on return and rolls back on unchecked exceptions
Checked exceptions commit unless `rollbackFor` says otherwise
`REQUIRED` joins, `REQUIRES_NEW` starts an independent transaction
Self-invocation bypasses the proxy and the annotation
pitfalls: Calling a @Transactional method from another method in the same class and expecting a new transaction.

quiz.q: A @Transactional method throws a checked IOException. What happens by default?
quiz.explain: Default rollback rules only cover unchecked exceptions; use rollbackFor to include checked ones.

concepts.name: Calling HTTP APIs with RestClient
concepts.summary: Call other services with the fluent RestClient and declarative @HttpExchange interfaces.
concepts.why: Microservices and integrations constantly call external HTTP APIs.
concepts.body:
Spring Framework 6.1 introduced **RestClient**, a fluent, synchronous HTTP client that replaces `RestTemplate` for new code (`RestTemplate` still works but is in maintenance mode). Spring Boot auto-configures a `RestClient.Builder` bean with the application's JSON message converters; inject the builder, set a base URL and defaults, and build a client:

```java
RestClient client = builder.baseUrl("https://api.example.com").build();
```

A call reads like the HTTP request: `client.get().uri("/users/{id}", id).retrieve().body(User.class)`. Use `toEntity` to get status and headers too, `body(new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<User>>() {})` for generic types, and `.post().body(dto)` to send JSON.

By default a 4xx or 5xx response throws `RestClientResponseException` (`HttpClientErrorException`/`HttpServerErrorException`). Customise with `onStatus(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError, (req, res) -> ...)`.

**HTTP interfaces** are a declarative alternative: annotate a Java interface with `@GetExchange("/users/{id}")` methods, then create an implementation with `HttpServiceProxyFactory` backed by a `RestClient`. The interface reads like a contract and is easy to mock in tests.

Always configure **timeouts** (connect and read) through the request factory, for example `ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings` or the `spring.http.client.*` properties in recent Boot versions; an unbounded call to a slow service ties up threads. For reactive apps use `WebClient` instead.
takeaways: RestClient is the modern synchronous client; RestTemplate is in maintenance
Inject Boot's `RestClient.Builder` to inherit JSON configuration
4xx/5xx throw by default; customise with `onStatus`
Always set connect and read timeouts
pitfalls: Creating `RestClient.create()` everywhere, losing Boot's configured converters, observability and timeouts.

quiz.q: What happens by default when retrieve().body(User.class) receives a 404?
quiz.explain: retrieve() treats 4xx and 5xx statuses as errors and throws unless onStatus handles them.

concepts.name: Actuator: health, metrics and info
concepts.summary: Expose health checks, metrics and runtime info for operating the app with Spring Boot Actuator.
concepts.why: Production systems need health probes, metrics and diagnostics; Actuator provides them out of the box.
concepts.body:
Add `spring-boot-starter-actuator` and the app gains management **endpoints** under `/actuator`. Only `health` is exposed over HTTP by default; expose more deliberately with `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus`.

Key endpoints:

- `/actuator/health` aggregates **health indicators**: database, disk space, Redis, message brokers, each auto-configured when the dependency is present. Show details with `management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized`. On Kubernetes, `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness` probe groups are enabled automatically.
- `/actuator/metrics` lists **Micrometer** metrics: JVM memory and GC, HTTP request timings (`http.server.requests`), connection pool usage. Adding `micrometer-registry-prometheus` exposes `/actuator/prometheus` for scraping.
- `/actuator/info` shows build and git information when configured; `loggers` changes log levels at runtime; `env`, `beans`, `mappings`, `configprops` and `threaddump` help debugging.

Record your own metrics by injecting `MeterRegistry` and creating counters and timers, or use the `@Observed` annotation with the Observation API for metrics plus traces. Write a custom `HealthIndicator` bean to report the state of a dependency Boot doesn't know about.

Endpoints like `env` and `heapdump` expose sensitive data: put the management port behind the firewall (`management.server.port`) or secure it with Spring Security.
takeaways: Actuator adds /actuator endpoints; only health is exposed by default
Health indicators are auto-configured for each dependency
Micrometer metrics export to Prometheus and other systems
Secure or isolate management endpoints
pitfalls: Exposing all endpoints (include=*) on the public port, leaking environment variables and heap dumps.

quiz.q: Which endpoint is exposed over HTTP by default after adding Actuator?
quiz.explain: Spring Boot exposes only the health endpoint over HTTP by default; others must be included explicitly.

concepts.name: Securing APIs with Spring Security
concepts.summary: Configure a SecurityFilterChain for authentication and authorization, including JWT resource servers.
concepts.why: Every real API needs authentication and authorization, and Spring Security is the standard.
concepts.body:
Adding `spring-boot-starter-security` secures **everything** immediately: all endpoints require authentication, with a generated password logged at startup and HTTP Basic plus a login form. That's a safe default; you then define what you actually want.

Security is a chain of servlet **filters** in front of the DispatcherServlet. Configure it by declaring a `SecurityFilterChain` bean using the lambda DSL on `HttpSecurity`:

- `authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll().requestMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE).hasRole("ADMIN").anyRequest().authenticated())` defines URL rules, evaluated in order.
- `httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())`, `formLogin(...)` or `oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))` choose how users authenticate.
- For stateless token-based APIs, disable sessions (`SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS`); CSRF protection can then be disabled because no cookies authenticate requests.

With a **JWT resource server** (`spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server`), set `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri` and Spring validates tokens from your identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Entra ID) on every request.

Method-level rules use `@EnableMethodSecurity` and `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #id == authentication.name")`. Inject the current user with `@AuthenticationPrincipal`. Store passwords only with a `PasswordEncoder` such as BCrypt. Test with `@WithMockUser` or `jwt()` request post-processors.
takeaways: Adding the starter secures everything; then you open up deliberately
Configure a `SecurityFilterChain` bean with the lambda DSL
Request matchers are evaluated in order; put specific rules first
JWT resource servers validate bearer tokens from an issuer
pitfalls: Disabling CSRF on an application that authenticates with session cookies, opening it to cross-site request forgery.

quiz.q: Rules are .anyRequest().authenticated() followed by .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll(). What happens?
options: It fails: anyRequest() must be the last rule
quiz.explain: Matchers are evaluated in order; Spring Security rejects configurations with rules after anyRequest().

concepts.name: How auto-configuration works
concepts.summary: Conditional configuration classes, @ConditionalOnMissingBean and the conditions report.
concepts.why: Knowing how Boot decides what to configure lets you override defaults confidently and debug startup.
concepts.body:
Auto-configuration is ordinary Spring configuration that Boot applies **conditionally**. Each auto-configuration class is listed in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` inside the Boot jars (and in third-party starters). At startup Boot loads the list and evaluates each class's conditions:

- `@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)`: only if a class is on the classpath. This is why adding a starter "turns on" a feature.
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`: only if you haven't defined your own bean of that type. This is the **back-off** rule that lets your configuration win.
- `@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "app.cache", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true")`: driven by configuration.
- `@ConditionalOnWebApplication`, `@ConditionalOnBean`, `@ConditionalOnResource` and more.

Auto-configurations are processed **after** your own configuration, so the conditions see your beans. Ordering between them uses `@AutoConfiguration(after = ...)`.

To customise, you rarely replace beans; first look for properties (`spring.jackson.*`) or **customizer** beans (`Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer`, `WebServerFactoryCustomizer`). Defining your own `ObjectMapper` or `DataSource` bean makes Boot's back off entirely. Exclude an auto-configuration with `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` or `spring.autoconfigure.exclude`.

Debug with `--debug` (or `debug=true`): the **conditions evaluation report** lists positive and negative matches with reasons. The `/actuator/conditions` endpoint shows the same at runtime.
takeaways: Auto-configurations are conditional `@Configuration` classes listed in `AutoConfiguration.imports`
`@ConditionalOnClass` reacts to the classpath; `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` lets your beans win
Prefer properties and customizer beans over replacing auto-configured beans
`--debug` prints the conditions evaluation report
pitfalls: Defining your own ObjectMapper bean to change one setting and losing all of Boot's Jackson configuration.

quiz.q: You define your own DataSource bean. What does DataSourceAutoConfiguration do?
options: Wraps your bean in a proxy
quiz.explain: Auto-configured beans are conditional on the absence of a user-defined bean of the same type.

concepts.name: JPA performance: N+1, fetching and projections
concepts.summary: Detect and fix N+1 queries, choose fetch strategies, and read data efficiently with projections and paging.
concepts.why: JPA hides SQL, and the queries it generates by default are the most common Spring performance problem.
concepts.body:
The **N+1 problem**: you load N orders with one query, then touching `order.getCustomer()` for each triggers N more queries. It's invisible in code and painful in production. Make it visible first: enable `spring.jpa.show-sql` or, better, log `org.hibernate.SQL` at DEBUG and count queries in tests.

Fetching rules:

- `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` are **eager** by default in JPA; mark them `fetch = FetchType.LAZY`. Collections (`@OneToMany`) are lazy.
- Load what a use case needs in one query with a **fetch join**, `select o from Order o join fetch o.customer`, or `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer")` on a repository method.
- `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` (e.g. 50) batches lazy loads into `IN` queries as a safety net.

Spring Boot enables **open-in-view** by default, keeping the persistence context open during view rendering so lazy loading works in controllers; it logs a warning at startup. Set `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false` so lazy loading outside transactions fails loudly instead of firing hidden queries.

For read-only screens, query **projections** instead of entities: an interface or record with just the needed columns (`List<BookSummary> findByAuthor(String a)`), avoiding dirty-checking overhead. Page large results with `Pageable` (`findAll(PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("title")))`); fetch-joining collections while paging forces in-memory pagination, so avoid that combination.
takeaways: N+1: one query for the list plus one per element; count queries to catch it
Make to-one associations LAZY and fetch per use case with join fetch or @EntityGraph
Disable open-in-view so hidden lazy loading fails fast
Use DTO projections and paging for read-heavy endpoints
pitfalls: Leaving @ManyToOne at its eager default, so every load of the entity pulls related rows you didn't need.

quiz.q: Loading 100 orders and reading order.getCustomer().getName() in a loop issues 101 queries. What fixes it in one query?
options: A join fetch or @EntityGraph on the query
quiz.explain: A fetch join (or entity graph) loads orders and customers together in a single SQL statement.

concepts.name: Integration tests with Testcontainers
concepts.summary: Run tests against real databases and brokers in Docker with Testcontainers and @ServiceConnection.
concepts.why: Tests against H2 miss database-specific behaviour; Testcontainers makes real dependencies cheap.
concepts.body:
In-memory databases behave differently from PostgreSQL or MySQL (SQL dialect, constraints, JSON types, locking), so tests pass and production fails. **Testcontainers** starts real services in throwaway Docker containers during tests.

Spring Boot integrates it tightly. Add `spring-boot-testcontainers` and the module you need (`org.testcontainers:postgresql`), then declare the container as a bean or static field annotated `@ServiceConnection`. Boot reads the container's host, port and credentials and configures the `DataSource` (or Kafka, Redis, MongoDB, RabbitMQ connections) automatically; no `@DynamicPropertySource` boilerplate.

Patterns:

- Annotate a test class with `@Testcontainers` and a `static @Container @ServiceConnection PostgreSQLContainer<?>` field; the container starts once for the class.
- Share containers across test classes by putting `@Bean @ServiceConnection` definitions in a `@TestConfiguration` class and importing it, so Spring's context cache reuses them.
- Combine with `@DataJpaTest` and `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)` for fast repository tests against the real database, running your Flyway migrations.

You can also use the same configuration at **development time**: a `TestApplication` main in `src/test` that calls `SpringApplication.from(App::main).with(ContainersConfig.class).run(args)` starts the app with its containers, replacing hand-maintained docker-compose files. Boot also supports Docker Compose directly with `spring-boot-docker-compose`.
takeaways: Testcontainers runs real dependencies in Docker for tests
`@ServiceConnection` configures connection properties automatically
Put containers in a shared `@TestConfiguration` to reuse them
The same setup can run the app locally
pitfalls: Starting a new container in every test class without sharing, making the suite slow.

quiz.q: What does @ServiceConnection on a PostgreSQLContainer bean do?
options: Tells Boot to derive DataSource connection details from the container
Starts PostgreSQL on the host machine
quiz.explain: Boot creates connection details from the running container, replacing manual spring.datasource properties.

concepts.name: Scheduling, async and virtual threads
concepts.summary: Run periodic jobs with @Scheduled, background work with @Async, and scale blocking code with virtual threads.
concepts.why: Background jobs and concurrency are part of most services, and Java 21 changes how you scale them.
concepts.body:
**Scheduling**: add `@EnableScheduling` to a configuration class and annotate methods with `@Scheduled(fixedRate = 60_000)`, `fixedDelay` (wait after completion), or `cron = "0 0 3 * * *"` (Spring's cron has six fields, starting with seconds). Durations like `fixedRateString = "PT1M"` or property placeholders keep schedules configurable. In a cluster every instance runs every job; use a lock such as ShedLock, or a dedicated scheduler, for jobs that must run once.

**Async methods**: `@EnableAsync` plus `@Async` on a bean method runs it on a task executor and returns immediately. Return `void` or `CompletableFuture<T>`. Like `@Transactional`, it works through proxies, so calls from the same class run synchronously. Boot auto-configures the executor (`spring.task.execution.pool.*`).

**Virtual threads** (Java 21+): set `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` and Boot runs Tomcat request handling, `@Async` tasks and scheduled tasks on virtual threads. Blocking I/O (JDBC, RestClient calls) then no longer pins a scarce platform thread, so a simple blocking-style service can handle many more concurrent requests without reactive programming.

Limits to know: the connection pool still caps concurrent database work, `synchronized` blocks around blocking calls can pin carrier threads on JDK 21-23 (fixed in JDK 24), and CPU-bound work gains nothing.
takeaways: `@Scheduled` with fixedRate, fixedDelay or six-field cron
`@Async` runs bean methods on an executor; return CompletableFuture
`spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` moves request handling to virtual threads
Every instance runs scheduled jobs; lock if they must run once
pitfalls: Calling an @Async method from the same class and wondering why it runs synchronously.

quiz.q: What does the Spring cron expression "0 */15 * * * *" mean?
quiz.explain: Spring cron has six fields starting with seconds, so this fires at second 0 of every 15th minute.

concepts.name: Bean lifecycle, proxies and AOP
concepts.summary: How the container creates beans, where BeanPostProcessors and proxies come in, and why self-invocation breaks.
concepts.why: Most baffling Spring bugs (annotations ignored, beans in odd states) come from lifecycle and proxy details.
concepts.body:
Creating a bean goes through defined phases: the container reads **bean definitions** (from scanning, `@Bean` methods, auto-configuration), lets `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`s modify the definitions (this is how `${...}` placeholders are resolved), then for each singleton: instantiate, inject dependencies, run **Aware** callbacks, call `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization`, run init callbacks (`@PostConstruct`, `afterPropertiesSet`), then `postProcessAfterInitialization`. On shutdown, `@PreDestroy` runs.

That last post-processing step is where **proxies** are created. Features like `@Transactional`, `@Async`, `@Cacheable`, `@Validated`, `@PreAuthorize` and custom `@Aspect`s are **AOP**: a post-processor wraps the bean in a proxy that runs the extra behaviour around method calls. Spring Boot uses CGLIB subclass proxies by default; JDK dynamic proxies are used only for interface-based proxying when configured.

Consequences:

- **Self-invocation**: `this.other()` inside the bean calls the target directly, not the proxy, so `other()`'s annotations do nothing. Restructure into a separate bean.
- CGLIB proxies can't intercept `final` or `private` methods, and a `final` class can't be proxied at all.
- The object injected elsewhere is the proxy, not your instance; `getClass()` shows a `$$SpringCGLIB$$` subclass.

Scopes other than singleton (`prototype`, `request`, `session`) also use proxies when injected into singletons. `@Configuration` classes are themselves CGLIB-enhanced so that calling one `@Bean` method from another returns the singleton; `proxyBeanMethods = false` turns this off for faster startup.
takeaways: BeanPostProcessors run around init callbacks; proxies are created after initialisation
Transactions, async, caching and security are proxy-based AOP
Self-invocation, final and private methods bypass proxies
`@Configuration` classes are proxied so @Bean methods return singletons
pitfalls: Marking a @Transactional or @Cacheable method private or final, so the proxy can't intercept it.

quiz.q: Why is helper()'s @Timed ignored when build() calls this.helper()?
options: @Timed only works on the first method
The call goes to the target object directly, bypassing the proxy
Aspects don't work on public methods
quiz.explain: Only calls coming through the proxy are intercepted; this.helper() is a plain Java call on the target.

concepts.name: Writing your own starter
concepts.summary: Package shared configuration as an auto-configuration module with conditions, properties and metadata.
concepts.why: Platform teams share logging, security and client setup across dozens of services through internal starters.
concepts.body:
When several services need the same setup (an HTTP client for an internal API, audit logging, a security baseline), package it as a **starter** so each service adds one dependency and gets sensible defaults it can override.

The conventional structure is two modules:

- `acme-audit-spring-boot-autoconfigure`: the `@AutoConfiguration` classes, `@ConfigurationProperties`, and the registration file `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` listing them, one fully qualified class name per line.
- `acme-audit-spring-boot-starter`: an empty jar whose POM depends on the autoconfigure module and the libraries it needs. Third-party starters are named `xxx-spring-boot-starter`; the `spring-boot-starter-*` prefix is reserved for official ones.

Design rules:

- Guard everything with conditions: `@ConditionalOnClass` for optional libraries, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` on every bean so applications can replace it, `@ConditionalOnProperty` for an on/off switch.
- Expose settings through a prefixed `@ConfigurationProperties` class and include `spring-boot-configuration-processor` so IDEs auto-complete them.
- Don't component-scan inside auto-configuration; declare beans explicitly. Use `@AutoConfiguration(after = ...)` to order relative to Boot's own.

Test it with `ApplicationContextRunner`, which starts tiny contexts in milliseconds and lets you assert which beans exist under different properties and classpaths (`FilteredClassLoader`).
takeaways: Split into an autoconfigure module and an empty starter POM
Register classes in `AutoConfiguration.imports`; don't rely on scanning
Make every bean `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` so apps can override
Test with `ApplicationContextRunner`
pitfalls: Naming an internal starter spring-boot-starter-foo, the prefix reserved for official Spring Boot starters.

quiz.q: How does Spring Boot discover your auto-configuration class in a starter jar?
quiz.explain: Boot loads auto-configuration class names from AutoConfiguration.imports files on the classpath.

concepts.name: Native images, AOT and startup tuning
concepts.summary: Compile Spring Boot apps ahead of time to GraalVM native images, and speed up JVM startup with CDS.
concepts.why: Fast startup and low memory matter for serverless, scale-to-zero and dense container deployments.
concepts.body:
A Spring app normally discovers beans, evaluates conditions and creates proxies at **runtime** with reflection, which costs startup time. Spring's **AOT (ahead-of-time) processing** moves that work to build time: it runs the application context in a special mode, then generates Java source code for the bean definitions, plus reflection, resource and proxy **hints** describing what needs to be reachable at runtime.

**GraalVM native image** compiles the app and the JDK into a standalone executable with a closed-world assumption: everything reachable must be known at build time. With the GraalVM Native Build Tools plugin, `./mvnw -Pnative native:compile` (or `./gradlew nativeCompile`, or `spring-boot:build-image -Pnative` for a container) produces a binary that starts in tens of milliseconds and uses far less memory. The costs: long builds, peak throughput often below a warmed-up JIT, and no runtime dynamism.

Restrictions follow from the closed world: the classpath and `@Profile`/`@ConditionalOnProperty` choices are fixed at build time, and reflection, resources, proxies and serialisation that Spring can't infer need hints via `RuntimeHintsRegistrar` and `@ImportRuntimeHints`, or `@RegisterReflectionForBinding`. Run tests natively (`-PnativeTest`) to catch missing hints.

Staying on the JVM, **Class Data Sharing** (CDS) cuts startup substantially with no code changes: extract the jar (`-Djarmode=tools extract`), do a training run with `-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh`, then start with `-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa`. Lazy initialisation (`spring.main.lazy-initialization=true`) helps too, at the cost of later errors.
takeaways: AOT processing generates bean definitions and runtime hints at build time
Native images start in milliseconds but fix the classpath and conditions at build time
Register hints for reflection and resources Spring can't infer
CDS speeds up JVM startup with no code changes
pitfalls: Relying on a runtime profile or property to switch beans in a native image; conditions were evaluated at build time.

quiz.q: Why does a native image need reflection hints?
options: GraalVM doesn't support reflection at all
Under the closed-world assumption only reflection known at build time is included
quiz.explain: Native image includes only reachable code and metadata; dynamic reflection must be declared ahead of time.
